q: על פי ה POCKET GUIDE TO THE 2019 AGS BEERS CRITERIA באיזה מהמצבים הבאים מתאים לטפל בתרופות אנטיפסיכוטיות באנשים מבוגרים?
o: טיפול בהפרעות התנהגות של דמנציה
טיפול במחלה ביפולרית
טיפול ממושך למניעת הקאות במקבלי כימותרפיה
טיפול קצר למניעת דליריום
explanation:
The supplementary check of **Beers 2023** identifies bipolar disorder as a recognized indication for antipsychotics in older adults. The exam originally cited the 2019 guide, which was not directly verified. Recognized indications must be distinguished from routine treatment of behavioral symptoms, which is restricted (pp. 2059–2060).

**A. Treatment of behavioral problems in dementia.** Wrong, routine use should be avoided; the source limits exceptions to specified circumstances involving nonpharmacologic measures and substantial risk of harm. Behavioral symptoms alone are insufficient (p. 2060).
**B. Treatment of bipolar disorder.** Correct, bipolar disorder is explicitly among approved indications excepted from the avoidance recommendation (p. 2059).
**C. Long-term prevention of vomiting during chemotherapy.** Wrong, the exception is short-term antiemetic use, not the proposed prolonged treatment (p. 2059).
**D. Short-term prevention of delirium.** Wrong, routine delirium prevention is not a recognized indication here; even treatment of existing delirium is subject to the defined exceptions (p. 2060).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2059–2060; the original 2019 reference was not directly verified.

q: בן 78, ברקע PAF, סוכרת, היפרליפידמיה, ומחלת לב איסכמית. התקבל למחלקת שיקום לאחר שהיה מאושפז במחלקה נוירולוגית עקב שבץ מוחי (CVA). בקבלתו לשיקום, הומלץ על טיפול ב- ATORVASTATIN (LIPITOR) במינון גבוה. הפיזיותרפיסט חושש שהטיפול בסטטינים יפגע בשרירים ויפריע לתהליך השיקומי. מה נכון לגבי מיופתיה על רקע שימוש ב- Lipid lowering agents ?
o: כ- 1% מהמטופלים בסטטינים יכולים לפתח רבדומיוליזיס
רוב המיופתיות מתייצגות תוך חודש מתחילת הטיפול בסטטינים
עליה של CPK נצפית בעד 10% מהמטופלים בסטטינים
טיפול ב- AMIODARONE יכול לעלות סיכון למיופתיה של סטטינים
explanation:
**Amiodarone** is among drugs involved in cytochrome P450 interactions, particularly CYP3A4, that increase the risk of statin-associated myopathy. The stem does not state that this patient takes amiodarone (Hazzard 8e, p. 1598).

**A. Approximately 1% of statin users develop rhabdomyolysis.** Wrong, the source describes rhabdomyolysis in approximately 0.1%; the option assigns this serious complication a higher frequency than the source (p. 1598).
**B. Most myopathies present within one month of starting a statin.** Wrong, median time to symptom onset is six months, and onset may occur after four years. One month is therefore not the window containing most cases (p. 1598).
**C. CPK elevation occurs in up to 10% of statin users.** Wrong, the book distinguishes myalgia with normal CK from myositis with elevated CK, described in approximately 1%; the option's frequency should not be assigned to enzyme elevation (p. 1598).
**D. Amiodarone can increase statin myopathy risk.** Correct, amiodarone is listed among drugs that may interact through statin metabolic pathways and increase myopathy risk, making this relevant to medication review (p. 1598).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 1598.

q:
בת 94, גרה לבדה עד האשפוז, לא ידוע על ירידה קוגניטיבית. מאושפזת במחלקה פנימית בשל אלח דם (SEPSIS) ממקור של דלקת בדרכי השתן. היא נושאת קתטר שתן ומטופלת באנטיביוטיקה דרך הוריד. רופא גריאטר נקרא לתת יעוץ בשל מצב של אי-שקט ובלבול. בבדיקה נראית כאובה, סובלת מאי שקט פסיכו-מוטורי בולט, ליקוי בקשב, חוסר התמצאות במקום ובזמן. רשימת תרופות שמקבלת:   
 ROCEPHIN  
 ENOXAPARIN (CLEXAN)  
 PARACETAMOL  
 OXAZEPAM (VABEN)  
 RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)  
 TROSPIUM (SPASMEX)  
 BROTIZOLAM (BONDORMIN)  
 מה צריך לייעץ בהתייחס לטיפול התרופתי שהמטופלת מקבלת?
o: להפסיק טיפול ב- VABEN שקיבלה בביתה
להפסיק את הטיפול ב- TROSPIUM (SPSMEX)
להחליף את ה-BROTIZOLAM (BONDORMIN) ב- ZOLPIDEM (ZODORM)
להוסיף טיפול קבוע ב- TRAMADOL לאיזון כאב
explanation:
The patient has a **delirium** presentation in the setting of sepsis and urinary infection: psychomotor agitation, impaired attention and disorientation. Older adults are vulnerable to anticholinergic adverse effects. Trospium is an anticholinergic bladder drug; its indication should be reviewed when reducing medication burden. A urinary catheter alone does not establish that it no longer has an indication (Hazzard 8e, pp. 888–889; Beers 2023, pp. 2066, 2074).

**A. Stop the oxazepam taken at home.** Wrong, prolonged benzodiazepine use may produce physical dependence. Inference: given that dependence and withdrawal can cause delirium, dose reduction should be planned according to the use history rather than automatically stopping abruptly (Beers, p. 2060; Hazzard, p. 889).
**B. Stop trospium.** Correct, this is the official answer. Trospium is listed among drugs with strong anticholinergic properties, a group that may worsen delirium (Beers, pp. 2066, 2074).
**C. Replace brotizolam with zolpidem.** Wrong, switching does not remove the delirium risk: Z-drugs are also associated with delirium (Beers, p. 2060).
**D. Add regular tramadol for pain.** Wrong, adding an opioid requires pain assessment and consideration of delirium risk, rather than automatic scheduled treatment (Beers, p. 2066).

Tramadol is an opioid that also inhibits serotonin reuptake. It can have central adverse effects and is not an automatic solution for pain during delirium; its mechanism should not be described as anticholinergic (Hazzard, p. 1061, Table 68-6).

Delirium management begins with nonpharmacologic approaches and includes reducing exposure to aggravating medications according to their indications (Hazzard, p. 888; Beers, p. 2066).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2060, 2066, 2074; Hazzard 8e, pp. 888–889, 1061.

q:
בן 82, פנה לרופא המשפחה עקב אירועים חוזרים של התעלפות. ברקע - סובל מיתר ל"ד, השמנת יתר, סוכרת ודמנציה. תרופות קבועות:   
 RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)  
 LERCANIDIPINE (VASODIP)  
 MEMANTIN (MEMOX)  
 DONEPEZIL (MEMORIT)  
 ATORVASTATIN (LIPITOR  
 אקו לב שנעשה לפני חודשיים תקין. במסגרת בירור נעשה הולטר שהדגים קטעים מרובים של: איזו מהתרופות הבאות מסבירה את הממצא באק"ג?
o: RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)
LERCANIDIPINE ( VASODIP)
MEMANTIN ( MEMOX)
DONEPEZIL ( MEMORIT)
explanation:
The supplied Holter strip shows a **prolonged pause between complexes** in the setting of recurrent syncope. An exact rhythm-subtype diagnosis is unnecessary for this drug comparison: the medication table explicitly lists bradycardia, heart block and syncope with **donepezil** (official Holter image; Hazzard 8e, p. 912).

**A. Ramipril (Tritace).** Wrong, this ACE inhibitor treats hypertension and cardiovascular conditions, but is not the drug explicitly associated here with the combination of bradycardia, block and syncope. Inference from the comparison and strip: donepezil fits better (pp. 1143, 912).
**B. Lercanidipine (Vasodip).** Wrong, this dihydropyridine calcium antagonist acts predominantly on vessels. Do not equate it automatically with heart-rate-slowing calcium antagonists; donepezil has the direct source link to bradycardia and block (lercanidipine SmPC, sections 4.1, 5.1; Hazzard p. 912).
**C. Memantine (Memox).** Wrong, the source offers memantine when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated because of bradycardia. This does not guarantee absence of cardiac effects, but supports donepezil as the clearer suspect among these drugs (pp. 911–913).
**D. Donepezil (Memorit).** Correct, the table lists bradycardia or heart block and syncope, fitting the recurrent fainting and prolonged pause (p. 912).

Sources: Hazzard 8e, pp. 911–913, 1143; Generics (UK) Ltd/Mylan, Lercanidipine hydrochloride 10 mg Summary of Product Characteristics, sections 4.1, 5.1, https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/102168/smpc.

q: בת 80 סובלת מאוסטאופורוזיס, TIA בעבר ו- GERD. מטופלת ב- ASPIRIN, ESOMEPRAZOLE (NEXIUM) ו- ALENDRONATE (FOSALAN).התקבלה למחלקה פנימית עקב שלשול ואובחנה כסובלת מזיהום על ידי CLOSTRIDIUM DEFICILLE. איזה מהבאים מגביר סיכון לחלות בזיהום ב- CLOSTRIDIUM DEFICILLE?
o: שימוש ממושך ב- ASPIRIN
שימוש ממושך ב- ESOMEPRAZOLE (NEXIUM)
שימוש ממושך ב- ALENDRONATE (FOSALAN)
שימוש ממושך בפרוביוטיקה
explanation:
**Proton pump inhibitors** are associated with increased C. difficile infection risk. The book suggests that acid suppression alters the gastrointestinal microbial environment. An observational association must be distinguished from proof of causation in this individual patient (Hazzard 8e, p. 1323).

**A. Long-term aspirin.** Wrong, the evidence overview reports no significant association between aspirin and community-associated CDI. Associations reported for other drugs should not automatically be extended to aspirin (Eze et al., 2017, Other drugs).
**B. Long-term esomeprazole.** Correct, it is a proton pump inhibitor, the class associated with increased enteric infections including C. difficile; this is the relevant issue when reviewing GERD treatment (Hazzard, p. 1323).
**C. Long-term alendronate.** Wrong according to the official key. An alendronate adverse-event reporting signal has been published, so it is inaccurate to say that no association has ever been reported. The authors call for cautious interpretation and further research; the signal alone does not prove causation (McConeghy et al., 2016, Abstract).
**D. Long-term probiotics.** Wrong, probiotics are discussed as an attempt to restore flora and as adjunctive treatment, not as acid suppression. The book does not establish proven efficacy for prevention or treatment, so protection should not be promised (Hazzard, pp. 1305, 1672).

Note: The question does not specify the required level of evidence. The PPI association must be distinguished from an adverse-event database signal (McConeghy et al., Abstract).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1305, 1323, 1672; Eze P et al. Risk factors for Clostridium difficile infections: an overview of the evidence base and challenges in data synthesis. J Glob Health. 2017;7:010417. doi:10.7189/jogh.07.010417, Other drugs; McConeghy KW et al. A Quantitative Analysis of FDA Adverse Event Reports with Oral Bisphosphonates and Clostridium difficile. Pharmacotherapy. 2016. doi:10.1002/phar.1832, Abstract.

q: בת 77 פונה להערכה גריאטרית כוללנית. באנמנזה תרופתית מדווח על שימוש ממושך ב- CLONAZEPAM (CLONEX) ומעוניינת להתייעץ לגבי הנזק בטיפול והחלופות אליו. מה השפעת הפרמקולוגיה של CLONAZEPAM לתופעות הלוואי שלה בקשישים?
o: עקב עליה בספיגה התחלת הפעילות מהירה יותר בקשישים
עקב עליה באחוז השומן בגוף זמן הפינוי של התרופה מהגוף ארוך יותר
עקב ירידה בפינוי הכלייתי יש צורך להפחית מינון בקשישים
בקשישים יש סיכון מוגבר להיווצרות מטבוליטים פעילים עם פינוי איטי
explanation:
Aging brings **relatively greater fat stores**, increasing the distribution volume of lipid-soluble benzodiazepines; drug absorption is generally unchanged (Hazzard 8e, p. 302). The accepted explanation is an **inference from drug distribution**, not a measurement of this patient's clonazepam kinetics. The label states that pharmacokinetics in older adults have not been established and that accumulation occurs with continued treatment (Rivotril Australian Product Information, section 5.2).

**A. Increased absorption causes faster onset in older adults.** Wrong, drug absorption is largely unchanged with age; the source does not support generally faster onset from increased absorption (p. 302).
**B. More body fat prolongs the drug's time in the body.** Correct under the key, as an application of the larger distribution volume of lipid-soluble benzodiazepines. Distinguish this inference from a quantitative claim about clonazepam clearance in older adults, which the label does not provide (p. 302; Rivotril section 5.2).
**C. Reduced renal clearance requires a dose reduction.** Wrong as the main pharmacokinetic explanation here because clonazepam is hepatically metabolized. However, metabolites can accumulate with renal impairment and warrant dose review; renal function is not irrelevant (Rivotril section 5.2).
**D. Increased formation of slowly cleared active metabolites.** Wrong, the described hepatic reduction produces pharmacologically inactive metabolites; prolonged effects should not be attributed to formation of active metabolites (Rivotril section 5.2).

Sources: Hazzard 8e, p. 302; Rivotril Australian Product Information, Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care, revised 18 March 2026, section 5.2 Pharmacokinetic Properties, https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/medicine-finder/rivotril.

q: בת 75, ברקע אי ספיקת לב, סוכרת, יתר לחץ דם, וזיהומים חוזרים בדרכי השתן עם טיפול אנטיביוטי מניעתי. פונה למרפאה בגין קשיי נשימה שהתחילו בצורה הדרגתית. בבדיקתה – סטורציה נמוכה, בהאזנה לריאות – קרפיטציות עדינות דו צדדיות בסוף אינספיריום. לאיזה מהתרופות שמקבלת יכול להיות קשר למחלתה?
o: AMLODIPINE
METFORMIN
SPIRONOLACTONE
NITOFURANTOIN
explanation:
**Official answer: ד — Nitrofurantoin.** Prolonged use is associated with pulmonary toxicity (Hazzard 8e, p. 1708).

**A. Amlodipine.** Wrong, this is not the drug identified by the source as long-term urinary prophylaxis with pulmonary toxicity; the exposure and symptoms point to nitrofurantoin (p. 1708).
**B. Metformin.** Wrong, it does not match the decisive exposure of prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis. This should not be read as a claim that the book excludes every possible pulmonary reaction to metformin (p. 1708).
**C. Spironolactone.** Wrong, underlying heart failure warrants considering other causes of dyspnea, but the explicit drug warning concerning urinary prophylaxis is for nitrofurantoin (p. 1708).
**D. Nitrofurantoin.** Correct, officially accepted; the book emphasizes pulmonary toxicity particularly with long-term use, linking the described exposure to the symptoms (p. 1708).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 1708.

q: בת 88 פנתה למיון עקב שקיעה במצב ההכרה. לפני שבוע נפלה ונחבלה וסבלה מכאבים קשים. המשפחה יודעת שהחולה לקחה תכשירים שונים לשיכוך כאב, ולאחר מכן הפכה להיות שקועה. המשפחה מביאה שקית עם תרופות אנלגטיות שונות אותן החולה לקחה בבית בשבוע האחרון. מי מבין התרופות האנלגטיות הבאות יכולה לגרום בסבירות גבוהה לשקיעה הכרתית?
o: ACAMOL FOCUS (PARACETAMOL, ASPIRIN, CAFFEINE)
COMBODEX (PARACETAMOL, IBUPROFEN)
MUSCOL (PARACETAMOL, ORPHENADRINE)
DIPYRONE (OPTALGIN)
explanation:
**Orphenadrine** is a skeletal muscle relaxant with anticholinergic effects and a risk of sedation in older adults. The Beers Criteria classify it as potentially inappropriate and recommend avoidance, supporting MUSCOL as the answer in this comparison (Beers 2023, pp. 2063, 2074).

**A. ACAMOL FOCUS (paracetamol, aspirin, caffeine).** Wrong, the listed formulation contains no orphenadrine. The supported explanation for sedation here is MUSCOL's anticholinergic muscle relaxant, rather than analgesic use itself (p. 2063).
**B. COMBODEX (paracetamol, ibuprofen).** Wrong, the table's main warnings for ibuprofen concern bleeding and kidney injury; orphenadrine is the component explaining sedation in this comparison (p. 2063).
**C. MUSCOL (paracetamol, orphenadrine).** Correct, it contains orphenadrine, explicitly listed among muscle relaxants poorly tolerated because of sedation and anticholinergic effects (pp. 2063, 2074).
**D. DIPYRONE (OPTALGIN).** Wrong, dipyrone is not the anticholinergic component identified here. This distinguishes the formulations in the question without claiming that other analgesics have no risks (pp. 2063, 2074).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2063, 2074 (PDF pp. 12, 23).

q: A 74-year-old woman with a previous hip fracture takes a long-acting benzodiazepine. Which rationale in Beers 2023 supports reducing exposure?
o: Increased sensitivity and slower metabolism of long-acting agents contribute to harm
Reduced sensitivity with age supports increasing the subsequent medication dose
Switching to a short-acting agent provides a demonstrated reduction in falls risk
Faster metabolism of long-acting agents explains the need for prolonged treatment
explanation:
**Benzodiazepines** pose particular problems in older adults because sensitivity increases and metabolism of long-acting agents decreases. The criteria associate the class with falls and fractures and state that shorter-acting agents are not safer (pp. 2060, 2066).
"Older adults have increased sensitivity to benzodiazepines and decreased metabolism of long-acting agents;" (p. 2060).
"Benzodiazepines: shorter-acting ones are not safer than long-acting ones." (p. 2066).

**A. Increased sensitivity and slower metabolism of long-acting agents contribute to harm.** Correct, this is the age-related sensitivity and metabolism pattern stated by the criteria (p. 2060).
**B. Reduced sensitivity with age supports increasing the subsequent medication dose.** Wrong, the source describes increased sensitivity, which argues against escalating treatment on the assumption of reduced sensitivity (p. 2060).
**C. Switching to a short-acting agent provides a demonstrated reduction in falls risk.** Wrong, the falls section explicitly states that shorter-acting benzodiazepines are not safer than long-acting ones (p. 2066).
**D. Faster metabolism of long-acting agents explains the need for prolonged treatment.** Wrong, the source describes decreased metabolism of long-acting agents, not faster metabolism (p. 2060).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2060, 2066.

q: According to the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, which effect supports avoiding concomitant opioid and benzodiazepine use in an older adult?
o: The combination may decrease sedation while depressing respiration
The combination may cause profound sedation and respiratory depression
The combination may cause profound sedation while stimulating respiration
The combination may decrease sedation while stimulating respiration
explanation:
Combining an opioid with a benzodiazepine creates a risk of **profound sedation and respiratory depression**, with potentially fatal outcomes. The Beers Criteria state: "Concomitant use of opioids may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death." (p. 2060).

**A. The combination may decrease sedation while depressing respiration.** Wrong, the source warns of profound sedation, rather than decreased sedation, with concomitant use (p. 2060).
**B. The combination may cause profound sedation and respiratory depression.** Correct, both effects are explicitly listed in the warning about concomitant opioid use (p. 2060).
**C. The combination may cause profound sedation while stimulating respiration.** Wrong, the warning describes respiratory depression, rather than stimulation of respiration (p. 2060).
**D. The combination may decrease sedation while stimulating respiration.** Wrong, both proposed directions conflict with the listed risks of profound sedation and respiratory depression (p. 2060).

Source: AGS Beers 2023, pp. 2060.

q: A 74-year-old man requests treatment for insomnia and asks about lorazepam. Which statement explains the Beers 2023 warning about benzodiazepines in older adults?
o: Choosing a short-acting agent reduces the risk of subsequent falls
Older adults have increased sensitivity and an increased risk of falls
Continued benzodiazepine use reduces the risk of physical dependence
Combining a benzodiazepine with an opioid reduces the risk of sedation
explanation:
**Benzodiazepine sensitivity** is increased in older adults, and this drug class increases the risk of falls and cognitive adverse effects. Short duration of action does not make a benzodiazepine safer for falls; continued use also carries a risk of physical dependence (pp. 2060, 2066).
"Older adults have increased sensitivity to benzodiazepines and decreased metabolism of long-acting agents;" (p. 2060).
"In general, all benzodiazepines increase the risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle crashes in older adults." (p. 2060).

**A. Choosing a short-acting agent reduces the risk of subsequent falls.** Wrong, Beers specifically states that shorter-acting benzodiazepines are not safer than long-acting ones in people with a history of falls or fractures (p. 2066).
**B. Older adults have increased sensitivity and an increased risk of falls.** Correct, Beers identifies increased sensitivity in older adults and includes falls among the risks of this drug class (p. 2060).
**C. Continued benzodiazepine use reduces the risk of physical dependence.** Wrong, continued use may lead to clinically significant physical dependence rather than protecting against it (p. 2060).
**D. Combining a benzodiazepine with an opioid reduces the risk of sedation.** Wrong, concomitant opioid use can cause profound sedation and respiratory depression, rather than reducing sedation (p. 2060).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2060, 2066.

q: An 82-year-old man with diabetes, multiple comorbidities, and limited life expectancy is reviewing his glycemic target. Which principle does Hazzard describe for setting the hemoglobin A1c goal?
o: Aim for a lower target as the burden of comorbid illness increases
Aim for a uniform target among patients of the same chronological age
Tailor the target to treatment goals, health status, and remaining life expectancy
Tailor the target to the laboratory normal range without weighing treatment risk
explanation:
**Individualized glycemic targets** balance treatment goals and health status with remaining life expectancy. Hazzard states that targets should reflect "the individual older adult’s treatment goals, health status, and remaining life expectancy" (p. 315). The rationale includes the higher hypoglycemia rates associated with tight glycemic control in older adults (p. 315).

**A. Aim for a lower target as the burden of comorbid illness increases.** Wrong, the cited guidance allows less stringent targets with multiple comorbidities and shorter life expectancy, rather than progressively lowering the target as illness burden increases (p. 315).
**B. Aim for a uniform target among patients of the same chronological age.** Wrong, the listed determinants vary between people of the same age; an age-based uniform target omits the individual health and goal assessment (p. 315).
**C. Tailor the target to treatment goals, health status, and remaining life expectancy.** Correct, these are the source's explicit determinants and directly address the comorbidity burden and limited life expectancy stated here (p. 315).
**D. Tailor the target to the laboratory normal range without weighing treatment risk.** Wrong, a laboratory reference range does not account for the treatment-related hypoglycemia concern or the source's individualized goals (p. 315).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 315.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q:
בת 85, ברקע דיכאון, פרפור עליות התקפי, היפרליפידמיה. אושפזה במחלקת פנימית גריאטרית בתמונה קלינית של דלקת ריאות. תרופות:  
 ECITRALOPAM 30 mg X1  
 AMIODARONE 200 mg X1  
 RIVAROXABAN 15 mg X1  
 הותחל טיפול ב- LEVOFLOXACIN (TAVANIC). יומיים לאחר האשפוז היא נמצאת מחוסרת הכרה במיטתה. הממצא במוניטור מופיע בתמונה 3. מספר תרופות אותן החולה מקבלת יכולות לגרום לתופעה זו. איזו תרופה לא גורמת לתופעה?
o: AMIODARONE
ECITRALOPAM
LEVOFLOXACIN
RIVAROXABAN
explanation:
The supplied rhythm strip is consistent with **polymorphic ventricular tachycardia**, suggesting torsade de pointes in this context. The drug comparison requires checking QT effects individually: rivaroxaban is an anticoagulant for which a dedicated QT study found no QTc-prolonging effect (official rhythm strip; Xarelto prescribing information, section 12.2).

**A. Amiodarone.** Wrong, its label warns of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QTc prolongation. An antiarrhythmic drug can still be proarrhythmic (amiodarone prescribing information, section 5.4).
**B. Escitalopram.** Wrong, its label describes QTc changes in an exposure study and reports of torsade de pointes; it cannot be selected as the drug unrelated to this phenomenon (escitalopram prescribing information, sections 6.1–6.2).
**C. Levofloxacin.** Wrong, the label links it to QT prolongation and torsade reports and cautions against use with QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics. Inference: its introduction is relevant to the combined medication risk here (levofloxacin prescribing information, section 5.11).
**D. Rivaroxaban.** Correct, it is an anticoagulant and the dedicated study found no QTc-prolonging effect, distinguishing it from the alternatives whose labels describe QT prolongation or torsade (Xarelto prescribing information, section 12.2).

**Official answer:** RIVAROXABAN (IMA final official answer key, December 2021 examination, question 77).

The textbook discusses direct oral anticoagulants and cardiac conduction effects of psychotropic drugs. The cited textbook passages do not provide a chain separately excluding the other three drugs and selecting rivaroxaban from the monitor finding (Hazzard 8e, pp. 929, 1204).

Sources: Aurobindo Pharma, amiodarone hydrochloride prescribing information (2022), section 5.4, https://www.dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/getFile.cfm?setid=7ae393d1-7469-432a-9f21-f5ebab1207d1&type=pdf. DailyMed/NLM, escitalopram prescribing information, sections 6.1–6.2, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=155e973a-f4ff-4e5a-b937-09f1e106fe39. DailyMed/NLM, levofloxacin prescribing information, section 5.11, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=f780bb91-483a-d1a6-e053-6294a90ab74b. Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Xarelto prescribing information, section 12.2, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=10db92f9-2300-4a80-836b-673e1ae91610.
explanationReviewNote: The source supports classifying rivaroxaban as an anticoagulant; reaching it by elimination also requires source-backed links from each of amiodarone, escitalopram and levofloxacin to the pictured rhythm, which it does not state.

q: Which benefit-risk profile does the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria describe for zolpidem in older adults?
o: Minimal improvement in sleep, with a risk of delirium and falls.
Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in fall risk.
Minimal improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.
Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.
explanation:
**Zolpidem** belongs to the nonbenzodiazepine benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics listed in Beers (p. 2060). The criteria describe "minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration" alongside adverse events including delirium, falls, and fractures, supporting the recommendation to avoid these agents in older adults (p. 2060).

**A. Minimal improvement in sleep, with a risk of delirium and falls.** Correct, the limited sleep benefit and the stated adverse events match the source (p. 2060).
**B. Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in fall risk.** Wrong, the source describes minimal benefit and falls as an adverse event, not substantial benefit with fall protection (p. 2060).
**C. Minimal improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.** Wrong, although the benefit is described as minimal, delirium is a listed adverse event rather than a risk reduced by treatment (p. 2060).
**D. Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.** Wrong, both parts conflict with the source: benefit is minimal, and delirium is an adverse event (p. 2060).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2060.

q: What is medication reconciliation, and why is it relevant when an older adult presents to the emergency department?
o: Compare the recorded medications with actual use to identify discrepancies and prevent medication errors
Compare the recorded diagnoses with recent laboratory results to establish disease severity and admission risk
Compare the recorded allergies with presenting symptoms to establish the reason for attendance and treatment sensitivity
Compare renal function with recommended drug doses to establish the dose limit for each recorded medication
explanation:
**Medication reconciliation** establishes an accurate list of what the patient takes, including dose, frequency, and route, and compares it with the medical record. Its purpose is to avoid omissions, duplication, dosing errors, and drug interactions during transitions of care (p. 311). "Medication reconciliation determines if the prescribed drugs are taken as they have been prescribed and intended." (p. 311)

**A. Compare the recorded medications with actual use to identify discrepancies and prevent medication errors.** Correct, this matches the comparison of the record with externally obtained medication information and its medication-safety purpose (p. 311).
**B. Compare the recorded diagnoses with recent laboratory results to establish disease severity and admission risk.** Wrong, comparing diagnoses and laboratory results does not establish what drugs the patient actually takes, which is the reconciliation task (p. 311).
**C. Compare the recorded allergies with presenting symptoms to establish the reason for attendance and treatment sensitivity.** Wrong, an allergy review does not by itself reconcile the list, doses, frequencies, and routes of medications actually used (p. 311).
**D. Compare renal function with recommended drug doses to establish the dose limit for each recorded medication.** Wrong, renal dose review examines one prescribing consideration; it does not establish and reconcile the full medication-use history (p. 311).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 311.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 77-year-old man has received androgen deprivation therapy for eight months. His son reports recent personality changes, irritability, and confusion fluctuating through the day. Oxybutynin was recently started for urinary urgency, and he takes diphenhydramine for sleep. He was previously cognitively well, and examination shows mild dehydration. Which interpretation of the oxybutynin–diphenhydramine combination matches Beers 2023?
o: Combined anticholinergic exposure reduces delirium risk while increasing fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure increases both delirium risk and fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure improves cognition while increasing fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure increases cognitive risk while reducing fall risk
explanation:
**Cumulative anticholinergic exposure** is relevant to this medication review. Oxybutynin and diphenhydramine are both listed as strongly anticholinergic; their combined use is associated with cognitive and fall-related harms (pp. 2070, 2074). "Use of more than one medication with anticholinergic properties increases the risk of cognitive decline, delirium, and falls or fractures." (p. 2070)

**A. Combined anticholinergic exposure reduces delirium risk while increasing fall risk.** Wrong, the table describes increased, not reduced, delirium risk with multiple anticholinergic drugs (p. 2070).
**B. Combined anticholinergic exposure increases both delirium risk and fall risk.** Correct, both named drugs have strong anticholinergic properties, and the combination fits the risk statement for delirium and falls (pp. 2070, 2074).
**C. Combined anticholinergic exposure improves cognition while increasing fall risk.** Wrong, the cognitive concern is decline and delirium, rather than cognitive improvement from this combination (p. 2070).
**D. Combined anticholinergic exposure increases cognitive risk while reducing fall risk.** Wrong, cognitive risk is correctly recognized, but the same interaction also increases rather than reduces fall risk (p. 2070).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2070, 2074.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2066, 2070, 2074, Tables 3, 5, 7

q: An 81-year-old woman with difficulty managing medications takes diphenhydramine nightly for sleep. Which consideration supports reviewing this medication under Beers 2023?
o: Cholinergic activity with a risk of confusion and constipation
Anticholinergic activity with a risk of confusion and constipation
Anticholinergic activity with a reduction in delirium risk
Cholinergic activity with a reduction in falling risk
explanation:
**Diphenhydramine** is listed among highly anticholinergic first-generation antihistamines. The criteria describe confusion and constipation and associate cumulative anticholinergic exposure with increased falls and delirium risk (p. 2057).
"Highly anticholinergic; clearance reduced with advanced age, and tolerance develops when used as hypnotic; risk of confusion, dry mouth, constipation, and other anticholinergic effects or toxicity." (p. 2057).
"Cumulative exposure to anticholinergic drugs is associated with an increased risk of falls, delirium, and dementia, even in younger adults." (p. 2057).

**A. Cholinergic activity with a risk of confusion and constipation.** Wrong, the listed pharmacologic property is anticholinergic, not cholinergic, although the proposed adverse symptoms are listed (p. 2057).
**B. Anticholinergic activity with a risk of confusion and constipation.** Correct, this matches the medication class and the adverse effects that warrant review in this patient (p. 2057).
**C. Anticholinergic activity with a reduction in delirium risk.** Wrong, the criteria associate anticholinergic exposure with increased, not decreased, delirium risk (p. 2057).
**D. Cholinergic activity with a reduction in falling risk.** Wrong, the property is anticholinergic, and cumulative exposure is associated with increased falls risk (p. 2057).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2057.

q: An 82-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease and osteoarthritis has increased evening confusion and fell a week ago. He takes donepezil 10 mg nightly, memantine 10 mg twice daily, acetaminophen 650 mg three times daily, and amitriptyline 50 mg nightly for chronic pain. Which action directly addresses a strongly anticholinergic medication exposure?
o: Move donepezil administration from evening to morning
Review discontinuation of amitriptyline used for pain
Reduce memantine to 5 mg twice daily
Add a low dose of quetiapine at dinner
explanation:
**Amitriptyline** is listed as a strongly anticholinergic antidepressant that should be avoided in older adults. The Beers rationale includes sedation and orthostatic hypotension; this supports reviewing its use without claiming it definitively caused the new confusion (p. 2059).
"Highly anticholinergic, sedating, and cause orthostatic hypotension" (p. 2059).

**A. Move donepezil administration from evening to morning.** Wrong, changing the timing of donepezil leaves the listed strongly anticholinergic antidepressant in place (p. 2059).
**B. Review discontinuation of amitriptyline used for pain.** Correct, this addresses the medication explicitly listed in the avoid category (p. 2059).
**C. Reduce memantine to 5 mg twice daily.** Wrong, reducing memantine leaves the amitriptyline exposure unaddressed (p. 2059).
**D. Add a low dose of quetiapine at dinner.** Wrong, adding an antipsychotic does not remove the anticholinergic exposure, and antipsychotics carry additional dementia-related risks (pp. 2059–2060).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2059, 2060.

q: A 76-year-old man is admitted to an Acute Care for Elders unit after a fall. Over two years he has developed confusion, become lost while driving, and had difficulty managing finances. He takes metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, simvastatin 40 mg daily, and temazepam 15 mg nightly. MMSE is 19/30 with impaired memory and orientation; MRI shows moderate hippocampal atrophy. His wife asks about memory medication. Which action addresses the benzodiazepine exposure associated with cognitive impairment and falls?
o: Add donepezil while retaining the current nightly temazepam.
Add memantine while retaining the current nightly temazepam.
Plan temazepam withdrawal after assessing physical dependence.
Add rivastigmine while retaining the current nightly temazepam.
explanation:
**Benzodiazepines**, including temazepam, increase risks of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, and fractures in older adults (p. 2060). Beers notes that "continued use of benzodiazepines may lead to clinically significant physical dependence" (p. 2060). The case application is to plan withdrawal of the potentially harmful exposure while assessing dependence, not to infer that abrupt cessation is appropriate.

**A. Add donepezil while retaining the current nightly temazepam.** Wrong, adding a cognitive drug leaves the benzodiazepine exposure and its listed risks in place (p. 2060).
**B. Add memantine while retaining the current nightly temazepam.** Wrong, adding memantine leaves the exposure associated with cognitive impairment and falls unchanged (p. 2060).
**C. Plan temazepam withdrawal after assessing physical dependence.** Correct, this addresses the exposure and the source's warning about dependence; the exact discontinuation schedule requires clinical assessment (p. 2060).
**D. Add rivastigmine while retaining the current nightly temazepam.** Wrong, changing cognitive treatment does not remove the benzodiazepine exposure named in the question (p. 2060).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2060.

q: An 84-year-old man with moderate vascular dementia, heart failure (ejection fraction 35%), and stage 3 CKD has slept more, eaten less, and stopped watching television over two weeks. He takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and citalopram 20 mg daily, started three weeks ago. He has flat affect and psychomotor slowing; sodium is 128, potassium 3.8, and creatinine 1.6. Which approach addresses a recognized medication-related contributor before attributing the change to chronic disease?
o: Attribute the change to dementia progression before reviewing recent medication effects
Assess hyponatremia associated with the recently introduced SSRI
Increase antidepressant treatment before reviewing recent medication effects and sodium
Attribute the change to heart failure before reviewing recent medication effects
explanation:
**SSRIs** carry a risk of hyponatremia: Hazzard states that "SSRIs carry risks of hyponatremia" (p. 1034). Rapid change over weeks also warrants review for medication effects, delirium, and medical illness (p. 904). In this vignette, considering citalopram as a contributor is an inference from the timing and low sodium, not proof of causation.

**A. Attribute the change to dementia progression before reviewing recent medication effects.** Wrong, the rapid time course requires assessment for medication effects and medical contributors before assuming dementia progression (p. 904).
**B. Assess hyponatremia associated with the recently introduced SSRI.** Correct, this evaluates an adverse effect explicitly recognized for SSRIs; attributing this individual case requires assessment (pp. 904, 1034).
**C. Increase antidepressant treatment before reviewing recent medication effects and sodium.** Wrong, escalation before reviewing the low sodium and recent drug exposure skips evaluation of a recognized adverse effect (pp. 904, 1034).
**D. Attribute the change to heart failure before reviewing recent medication effects.** Wrong, heart failure does not remove the need to assess reversible medication-related contributors to a rapid change (p. 904).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 904, 1034.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 75-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (eGFR 42) has increased evening confusion and two episodes of urinary incontinence. He takes donepezil 10 mg nightly, memantine 10 mg twice daily, and oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, started one month ago for urgency. Examination is normal and urinalysis is negative. Which approach directly addresses a possible adverse effect of the newly added bladder medication?
o: Review and trial discontinuation of oxybutynin as a possible contributor.
Continue oxybutynin and increase its dose to address the incontinence.
Continue oxybutynin and add a cognitive drug before reviewing its effects.
Continue oxybutynin and attribute the confusion to dementia progression.
explanation:
**Medication review** should examine symptom timing relative to recent changes; anticholinergic drugs can contribute to confusion or agitation (p. 922). Hazzard states, "Each new symptom should prompt a medication review and a trial of discontinuation of the suspected agent" (p. 121). Oxybutynin has anticholinergic adverse effects including delirium (p. 712); considering it a contributor here is an inference, not proof of causation.

**A. Review and trial discontinuation of oxybutynin as a possible contributor.** Correct, this applies the recommended review and trial withdrawal of a suspected agent to the recently introduced anticholinergic (pp. 121, 712, 922).
**B. Continue oxybutynin and increase its dose to address the incontinence.** Wrong, increasing exposure does not address a suspected adverse effect of that exposure; the source advises reviewing and trialing withdrawal of the suspected agent (p. 121).
**C. Continue oxybutynin and add a cognitive drug before reviewing its effects.** Wrong, adding treatment before reviewing the suspected agent risks treating an adverse effect with another drug, the prescribing cascade described in the source (p. 121).
**D. Continue oxybutynin and attribute the confusion to dementia progression.** Wrong, the source requires attention to recent medication changes before attributing behavioral symptoms to other causes (p. 922).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 121, 712, 922.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 79-year-old man with heart failure and cognitive impairment struggles with a complex medication regimen after discharge. Review identifies nonessential drugs and administration times that can be combined. Which structural change follows Hazzard's prescribing principles?
o: Add separate administration times to create more reminders
Retain nonessential medications to preserve familiar habits
Remove nonessential medications and combine administration times
Separate administration times to practice independent management
explanation:
**Regimen complexity** is associated with poorer adherence and more adverse medication effects. Hazzard recommends the simplest effective regimen and discontinuation of unnecessary drugs; the stem specifies that the identified administration times can be combined (pp. 313–314). "The goal should thus be to implement the simplest regimen that controls the patient’s symptoms and illnesses, and optimizes disease prevention." (p. 313).

**A. Add separate administration times to create more reminders.** Wrong, adding administration times increases complexity rather than implementing the simplest effective regimen (p. 313).
**B. Retain nonessential medications to preserve familiar habits.** Wrong, preserving nonessential drugs conflicts with the instruction to consider discontinuing unnecessary drugs (p. 314).
**C. Remove nonessential medications and combine administration times.** Correct, this removes unnecessary treatment and reduces complexity where the review has established that consolidation is feasible (pp. 313–314).
**D. Separate administration times to practice independent management.** Wrong, splitting feasible shared times increases complexity, which the source links to poorer adherence and more adverse effects (p. 313).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 313, 314.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 78-year-old woman takes nitrofurantoin daily for long-term suppression of recurrent urinary tract infections. Her creatinine clearance is 42 mL/min. According to the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, which recommendation addresses the long-term suppression?
o: Stop long-term suppression and reassess the prevention plan
Continue long-term suppression with periodic renal-function monitoring
Reduce the daily dose and continue long-term suppression
Give the dose in the evening and continue long-term suppression
explanation:
**Long-term nitrofurantoin suppression** is discouraged because of pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy. The Beers recommendation to avoid prolonged suppression is separate from the creatinine-clearance restriction (p. 2057).
"Avoid in individuals with CrCl <30 mL/ min or for long-term suppression." (p. 2057).

**A. Stop long-term suppression and reassess the prevention plan.** Correct, this addresses the recommendation to avoid long-term suppression (p. 2057).
**B. Continue long-term suppression with periodic renal-function monitoring.** Wrong, renal monitoring does not remove the separate recommendation against long-term suppression (p. 2057).
**C. Reduce the daily dose and continue long-term suppression.** Wrong, lowering the dose does not address the recommendation to avoid the prolonged suppressive course (p. 2057).
**D. Give the dose in the evening and continue long-term suppression.** Wrong, changing the time of administration does not address the risk of long-term use (p. 2057).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2057.

q: A 79-year-old woman is brought by her daughter for routine follow-up. She has fallen twice in the past month and seems more forgetful. She lives alone and manages her finances, but recently burned a pot while cooking. She takes donepezil 10 mg daily, amitriptyline 50 mg at night for neuropathic pain, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Blood pressure is 128/78 sitting and 108/65 after three minutes standing. Her Mini-Cog score is 2/5. Which approach to amitriptyline addresses the medication concern identified in Beers 2023?
o: Retain amitriptyline because it has little effect on standing blood pressure
Review amitriptyline for discontinuation because of anticholinergic and orthostatic effects
Increase amitriptyline because stronger anticholinergic activity supports cognitive function
Replace amitriptyline with imipramine to avoid the strongly anticholinergic antidepressant group
explanation:
**Amitriptyline** is strongly anticholinergic and sedating and can cause orthostatic hypotension. Beers recommends avoiding this antidepressant group, which also includes imipramine (p. 2059).
"Highly anticholinergic, sedating, and cause orthostatic hypotension;" (p. 2059).
"Antidepressants with strong anticholinergic activity, alone or in combination" (p. 2059).

**A. Retain amitriptyline because it has little effect on standing blood pressure.** Wrong, orthostatic hypotension is explicitly part of the rationale for avoiding the drug group (p. 2059).
**B. Review amitriptyline for discontinuation because of anticholinergic and orthostatic effects.** Correct, it addresses the properties identified by the criterion without claiming a proven ranking of fall-prevention interventions (p. 2059; application).
**C. Increase amitriptyline because stronger anticholinergic activity supports cognitive function.** Wrong, strong anticholinergic activity is a reason for avoidance, not a rationale for increasing treatment to support cognition (p. 2059).
**D. Replace amitriptyline with imipramine to avoid the strongly anticholinergic antidepressant group.** Wrong, imipramine is in the same group, so the substitution does not avoid strongly anticholinergic antidepressants (p. 2059).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2059.

q: A 91-year-old woman with vascular dementia and chronic kidney disease develops acute confusion in assisted living. Evaluation finds no urinary symptoms, fever, or hemodynamic instability. Urinalysis shows pyuria and a few bacteria, and nitrofurantoin was started for suspected UTI. Which approach follows the source’s advice about nonspecific symptoms without localizing evidence of UTI?
o: Continue nitrofurantoin and add medication for agitation
Replace nitrofurantoin with a broader-spectrum antibiotic
Stop nitrofurantoin, monitor, and evaluate other causes
Continue nitrofurantoin while awaiting a urine culture
explanation:
**Confusion and abnormal urine findings do not by themselves establish symptomatic UTI.** Hazzard states that "unless more specific localizing signs and symptoms for UTI are present, clinicians should NOT initiate UTI treatment for these symptoms." (p. 1703). Monitoring should accompany evaluation for other causes of the acute change (pp. 885, 1703).

**A. Continue nitrofurantoin and add medication for agitation.** Wrong, continuing antibiotic treatment lacks the localizing evidence required by the source; treating agitation does not resolve that diagnostic gap (pp. 885, 1703).
**B. Replace nitrofurantoin with a broader-spectrum antibiotic.** Wrong, broadening antibiotics does not supply evidence that the urinary tract is the cause of the confusion (p. 1703).
**C. Stop nitrofurantoin, monitor, and evaluate other causes.** Correct, this applies the no-treatment principle to an antibiotic already started without supporting symptoms, while continuing assessment and observation (pp. 885, 1703; clinical application).
**D. Continue nitrofurantoin while awaiting a urine culture.** Wrong, waiting for a culture does not justify continuing treatment for nonspecific confusion without localizing urinary symptoms (p. 1703).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 885, 1703.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: גבר בן 84 עם heart failure (EF 35%) ו-CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22) מגיע לקליניקה. אשתו מדווחת שהוא מבולבל יותר בימים האחרונים וישן במהלך היום. התרופות כוללות furosemide 80mg BID, spironolactone 25mg daily, metoprolol 50mg BID, ו-gabapentin 300mg TID לנוירופתיה. תוצאות מעבדה: K+ 5.8, Na+ 134, BUN 78, Cr 3.2. איזו התאמה תרופתית היא המתאימה ביותר?
o: הפסקת spironolactone
הפחתת gabapentin ל-300mg daily
החלפת furosemide ב-bumetanide
הפחתת metoprolol ל-25mg BID
explanation:
התשובה הנכונה היא הפחתת gabapentin ל-300mg daily. עם eGFR של 22, gabapentin מחייב הפחתת מינון משמעותית (מקסימום 300mg daily ב-CKD stage 4). הצטברות gabapentin גורמת ל-sedation, delirium ושיבוש מחזור שינה-ערות — מה שמסביר את הסימפטומים של המטופל.

אופציה א' (הפסקת spironolactone) היא ה-trap answer. למרות שהיפרקלמיה מצביעה על צורך בהפחתת spironolactone, היא אינה מסבירה את הסימפטומים הנוירולוגיים. קלינאים רבים מתמקדים בערך המעבדה החריג במקום לקשר את הסימפטומים לרעילות תרופתית.

אופציה ג' (החלפת משתנים) אינה מטפלת בתלונה המרכזית של delirium וישנוניות יממית, אף שרוטציה של loop diuretics יכולה לסייע בהתנגדות למשתנים.

אופציה ד' (הפחתת metoprolol) עלולה להחמיר את שליטת ה-heart failure מבלי לטפל בגורם הסביר לסימפטומים.

Clinical Pearl: Gabapentin ו-pregabalin מחייבים הפחתת מינון אגרסיבית ב-CKD — 50% מינון ב-CKD3, 25% ב-CKD4, ו-10-15% ב-CKD5. הצטברות מתבטאת כ-'gabapentin encephalopathy' עם delirium, somnolence ומיוקלונוס. יש לחשב מחדש מינונים בכל שינוי בתפקוד הכליות.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING
retiredReason: Two defensible answers by Hazzard pp. 1181-1182; a look-alike question teaches the opposite.

q: A 91-year-old woman with moderate dementia has increasing agitation and refuses medication. She has round-the-clock caregivers, an MMSE score of 14/30, and needs assistance with all activities of daily living. Her family requests risperidone. Her daughter, the healthcare proxy, says, "We want her comfortable without hastening her death." Which approach follows the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Begin risperidone before behavioral approaches, relying on continuous supervision for safety.
Discuss stroke and mortality risks and assess nonpharmacologic approaches before prescribing.
Substitute scheduled lorazepam before behavioral approaches, relying on its cognitive safety.
Begin risperidone without a risk discussion, relying on comfort as sufficient justification.
explanation:
**Antipsychotics in dementia** are associated with "Increased risk of stroke and greater rate of cognitive decline and mortality in persons with dementia" (p. 2059). Beers advises avoiding them for behavioral problems unless specified conditions involving nonpharmacologic treatment failure or substantial harm are met (p. 2066). The stated presentation does not establish those conditions; discussing risks and nonpharmacologic options therefore follows the criteria.

**A. Begin risperidone before behavioral approaches, relying on continuous supervision for safety.** Wrong, continuous supervision does not replace the criteria concerning nonpharmacologic options and substantial harm (p. 2066).
**B. Discuss stroke and mortality risks and assess nonpharmacologic approaches before prescribing.** Correct, this addresses the stated risks and the conditions for considering an antipsychotic for dementia-related behavior (pp. 2059, 2066).
**C. Substitute scheduled lorazepam before behavioral approaches, relying on its cognitive safety.** Wrong, benzodiazepines also carry adverse CNS effects in dementia; substituting one does not establish a cognitively safe approach (p. 2066).
**D. Begin risperidone without a risk discussion, relying on comfort as sufficient justification.** Wrong, a comfort goal does not remove the documented stroke, cognitive, and mortality risks or the prescribing conditions (pp. 2059, 2066).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2059, 2066.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp.2059, 2066, Tables 2–3

q: An older adult with delirium has ranitidine on the home medication list. Ranitidine is no longer named in the delirium row of the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria. How should this omission be interpreted?
o: Its omission reflects evidence supporting its use at lower levels of renal function.
Its omission reflects incorporation of its warning into the general opioid category.
Its omission reflects U.S. market removal despite continued classification as potentially inappropriate.
Its omission reflects a recommendation to monitor delirium while continuing the lowest dose.
explanation:
**Removal from a table is not evidence of safety.** Table 8 lists ranitidine under delirium with the reason "Removed from the U.S. market" (p. 2075). The footnote states that drugs removed for low use or U.S. unavailability remain potentially inappropriate under the earlier recommendations; the H2-receptor antagonist delirium warning remains in Table 3 (pp. 2066, 2076).

**A. Its omission reflects evidence supporting its use at lower levels of renal function.** Wrong, the renal-function evidence explanation belongs to the apixaban criterion; the ranitidine entry instead gives U.S. market removal as its reason (pp. 2075–2076).
**B. Its omission reflects incorporation of its warning into the general opioid category.** Wrong, the opioid-category explanation belongs to meperidine, whereas ranitidine has a separate market-removal explanation (p. 2075).
**C. Its omission reflects U.S. market removal despite continued classification as potentially inappropriate.** Correct, the ranitidine entry and the Table 8 footnote together explain why omission does not remove its earlier potentially inappropriate designation (pp. 2075–2076).
**D. Its omission reflects a recommendation to monitor delirium while continuing the lowest dose.** Wrong, the lowest-dose, shortest-duration and monitoring advice is the corticosteroid qualification; it is not the reason given for removing ranitidine (pp. 2066, 2075).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2075, 2076, 2066.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2066, 2075–2076; Tables 3 and 8

q: A 79-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension presents after a mechanical fall. She takes metformin, glyburide 10 mg twice daily, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and aspirin. BP is 142/88 and glucose is 52. She reports recurrent dizziness and near-falls. Creatinine is 1.3, eGFR 44, and Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance 38 mL/min. After treating the hypoglycemia, which assessment of glyburide accords with the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Continue glyburide because long-acting sulfonylureas have less prolonged hypoglycemia
Increase glyburide because sulfonylureas protect against hypoglycemia compared with alternatives
Discontinue glyburide and reassess treatment because of its prolonged-hypoglycemia risk
Continue glyburide because it is the short-acting agent preferred within this class
explanation:
**Glyburide** is a long-acting sulfonylurea with a higher risk of prolonged hypoglycemia than short-acting agents (p. 2061). Beers advises avoiding sulfonylureas as initial or add-on treatment unless there are substantial barriers to safer alternatives (p. 2061). The source notes: "glyburide, glimepiride) confer a higher risk of prolonged hypoglycemia than short-acting agents (e.g., glipizide)." (p. 2061). Reassessment after the documented low glucose is an application of that safety concern, not proof that every fall was caused by glyburide.

**A. Continue glyburide because long-acting sulfonylureas have less prolonged hypoglycemia.** Wrong, the stated comparison runs in the opposite direction: long-acting agents carry greater prolonged-hypoglycemia risk (p. 2061).
**B. Increase glyburide because sulfonylureas protect against hypoglycemia compared with alternatives.** Wrong, sulfonylureas have higher hypoglycemia risk than alternative agents, so this rationale for increasing glyburide conflicts with the source (p. 2061).
**C. Discontinue glyburide and reassess treatment because of its prolonged-hypoglycemia risk.** Correct, withdrawing the implicated long-acting drug and reassessing treatment addresses its recognized risk after this episode (p. 2061; application).
**D. Continue glyburide because it is the short-acting agent preferred within this class.** Wrong, glyburide is classified as long-acting; glipizide is the short-acting example preferred if a sulfonylurea is used (p. 2061).

Source: AGS Beers 2023, pp. 2061.

q: An 86-year-old man from assisted living presents with acute confusion and a positive CAM. At 3 a.m. he tried to leave for work. He has mild dementia, insomnia, and osteoarthritis. Six hours earlier he received tramadol 100 mg, trazodone 100 mg, and diphenhydramine 50 mg. Vital signs are normal. Which concern about oral diphenhydramine is specifically identified by the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Its clearance increases with advancing age, reducing anticholinergic exposure.
Its anticholinergic effects carry a risk of confusion and delirium.
Its regular use as a hypnotic preserves responsiveness without tolerance.
Its use during delirium is favored because of protective cognitive effects.
explanation:
**Oral diphenhydramine** is listed among first-generation antihistamines to avoid because of substantial anticholinergic effects, reduced clearance with advanced age, and risk of confusion (p. 2057). Anticholinergics can induce or worsen **delirium**, so Beers recommends avoiding them in older adults with or at high risk of delirium (p. 2066).
"Highly anticholinergic; clearance reduced with advanced age, and tolerance develops when used as hypnotic; risk of confusion, dry mouth, constipation, and other anticholinergic effects or toxicity." (p. 2057).

**A. Its clearance increases with advancing age, reducing anticholinergic exposure.** Wrong, Beers describes reduced clearance with advanced age, not increased clearance; the proposed pharmacokinetic explanation conflicts with that description (p. 2057).
**B. Its anticholinergic effects carry a risk of confusion and delirium.** Correct, confusion is an explicit anticholinergic risk, and anticholinergics can induce or worsen delirium; these are relevant medication concerns in this presentation (pp. 2057, 2066).
**C. Its regular use as a hypnotic preserves responsiveness without tolerance.** Wrong, Beers states that tolerance develops when these antihistamines are used as hypnotics, so sustained responsiveness without tolerance is not the stated rationale (p. 2057).
**D. Its use during delirium is favored because of protective cognitive effects.** Wrong, the recommendation is to avoid anticholinergics in patients with delirium because they can induce or worsen it, rather than use them for cognitive protection (p. 2066).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria, 2023, pp. 2057, 2066.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2057, 2066, Tables 2–3

q: A 77-year-old man with diabetes, coronary artery disease, and depression presents with dizziness and weakness. He takes metformin, atorvastatin, metoprolol 100 mg twice daily, lisinopril, paroxetine 40 mg daily, and recently added amitriptyline 75 mg for neuropathy. BP is 102/68 seated and 84/52 standing, heart rate is 58, and QTc is 492 ms. Which assessment of amitriptyline follows from the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Continue it for its cholinergic activity and protection against postural hypotension
Continue it for its stimulating activity and protection against daytime sedation
Avoid it because of anticholinergic activity, sedation, and orthostatic hypotension
Increase it because postural hypotension indicates a need for more anticholinergic activity
explanation:
**Amitriptyline** belongs to the strongly anticholinergic antidepressants that Beers recommends avoiding (p. 2059). The listed rationale is "Highly anticholinergic, sedating, and cause orthostatic hypotension" (p. 2059). This supports reviewing amitriptyline in the described regimen without using the page to establish which of several drugs is the single most urgent cause of all findings.

**A. Continue it for its cholinergic activity and protection against postural hypotension.** Wrong, the drug is strongly anticholinergic and can cause orthostatic hypotension; the proposed protective profile is contrary to the source (p. 2059).
**B. Continue it for its stimulating activity and protection against daytime sedation.** Wrong, the source describes a sedating drug, not a treatment that protects against sedation through stimulation (p. 2059).
**C. Avoid it because of anticholinergic activity, sedation, and orthostatic hypotension.** Correct, this reproduces the recommendation and its three-part rationale (p. 2059).
**D. Increase it because postural hypotension indicates a need for more anticholinergic activity.** Wrong, postural hypotension is part of the avoidance rationale, not a rationale for increasing the drug (p. 2059).

Source: AGS Beers 2023, pp. 2059.

q: A woman with falls takes zolpidem. Her team considers switching to a short-half-life benzodiazepine on the assumption that a shorter duration prevents fall injuries. Which conclusion follows Hazzard?
o: A shorter half-life indicates a low risk of fall injuries
A shorter half-life justifies less frequent medication review
A shorter half-life does not establish a lower risk of fall injuries
A shorter half-life identifies a treatment that does not contribute to falls
explanation:
**Half-life does not establish clinical safety** in this comparison. Hazzard reports that fall-related injury risk with short-half-life benzodiazepines and Z-drugs may be similar to that with long-half-life benzodiazepines (p. 303).
"the risk of fall-related injuries in older adults prescribed short half-life benzodiazepines and so-called “Z-drugs” (eg, zolpidem) may actually be similar to that of long-half-life benzodiazepines." (p. 303).

**A. A shorter half-life indicates a low risk of fall injuries.** Wrong, the reported similarity in injury risk does not support classifying the short-half-life drug as low risk (p. 303).
**B. A shorter half-life justifies less frequent medication review.** Wrong, half-life does not resolve the fall-risk concern, so reduced review is not supported by this comparison (inference, p. 303).
**C. A shorter half-life does not establish a lower risk of fall injuries.** Correct, this preserves the uncertainty and possible similarity in risk described by the source (p. 303).
**D. A shorter half-life identifies a treatment that does not contribute to falls.** Wrong, a shorter half-life does not establish absence of contribution to fall injuries (p. 303).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 303.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes takes insulin glargine. Recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia is documented, and HbA1c is below his individualized target. After treating the acute episodes, what direction of treatment adjustment is appropriate?
o: Reduce treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response
Increase treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response
Maintain treatment intensity and target a lower HbA1c
Add an insulin secretagogue and monitor the glucose response
explanation:
**Overly tight glycemic control** increases hypoglycemia in older adults. Applying the source's dose-reduction principle to recurrent hypoglycemia with HbA1c below the individualized target supports reducing treatment intensity; glucose monitoring assesses the response and detects further hypoglycemia (pp. 315, 1574).
"Tight glycemic control has been consistently shown to produce higher rates of hypoglycemia in older adults." (p. 315).
"In some cases, there will be a need to deprescribe drug therapy by reducing the dose or stopping the medication entirely." (p. 315).

**A. Reduce treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response.** Correct, this addresses the excessive treatment intensity indicated by the supplied hypoglycemia and below-target HbA1c (pp. 315, 1574).
**B. Increase treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response.** Wrong, increasing intensity would pursue still tighter control despite the hypoglycemia associated with that approach (p. 315).
**C. Maintain treatment intensity and target a lower HbA1c.** Wrong, a lower HbA1c target fails to address the adverse effect already occurring with below-target control (p. 315).
**D. Add an insulin secretagogue and monitor the glucose response.** Wrong, adding glucose-lowering treatment intensifies the regimen rather than applying the dose-reduction approach to the documented adverse effect (p. 315).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 315, 1574.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: An 81-year-old woman in assisted living is assessed because her care needs have increased. She has moderate Alzheimer disease, osteoporosis with a recent vertebral fracture, and urinary incontinence. Her caregiver reports new dependence in bathing and dressing, previously performed independently, and two falls this month. Her medicines are donepezil 10 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, and acetaminophen as needed. Which response to oxybutynin matches Beers 2023?
o: Continue oxybutynin because its adverse effects are confined to the urinary tract
Review oxybutynin for discontinuation because of adverse cognitive effects
Increase oxybutynin because stronger anticholinergic activity protects cognitive function
Switch bladder antimuscarinics because the cognitive warning does not extend across the class
explanation:
**Bladder antimuscarinics** have potential anticholinergic effects, and oxybutynin has the best evidence for adverse cognitive effects in this group. Beers recommends avoiding anticholinergics in dementia or cognitive impairment because of adverse CNS effects (pp. 2066, 2074).
"Oxybutynin has the best evidence for adverse cognitive effects." (p. 2074).
"However, caution is warranted for all bladder antimuscarinics given their potential anticholinergic effects." (p. 2074).

**A. Continue oxybutynin because its adverse effects are confined to the urinary tract.** Wrong, adverse cognitive effects show that the relevant harms extend beyond the urinary tract (p. 2074).
**B. Review oxybutynin for discontinuation because of adverse cognitive effects.** Correct, it applies the cognitive-impairment criterion to oxybutynin without promising reversal of all functional decline (pp. 2066, 2074).
**C. Increase oxybutynin because stronger anticholinergic activity protects cognitive function.** Wrong, anticholinergic activity is the cognitive concern in this criterion, not a protective effect (pp. 2066, 2074).
**D. Switch bladder antimuscarinics because the cognitive warning does not extend across the class.** Wrong, Beers urges caution for all bladder antimuscarinics; changing within the class does not justify dismissing the warning (p. 2074).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2066, 2074.

q: An 86-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson disease, depression, and recurrent urinary tract infections attends follow-up. She lives in assisted living, uses a wheelchair, and has mild dysphagia. Her daughter reports worsening tremor and two falls this month. Medicines are carbidopa-levodopa 25/250 mg four times daily, pramipexole 1 mg three times daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and nitrofurantoin 100 mg daily for prophylaxis. Her creatinine clearance is 28 mL/min. Which statement about nitrofurantoin follows Beers 2023?
o: Continue nitrofurantoin because long-term suppression reduces the pulmonary and hepatic toxicity risks
Avoid nitrofurantoin because kidney function and long-term use meet avoidance criteria
Continue nitrofurantoin because the avoidance criteria are independent of the level of kidney function
Continue nitrofurantoin because the toxicity concerns primarily concern short courses rather than prolonged use
explanation:
**Nitrofurantoin** is recommended for avoidance when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min or when used for long-term suppression. Beers cites pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy, particularly with long-term use (p. 2057).
"Avoid in individuals with CrCl <30 mL/ min or for long-term suppression." (p. 2057).
"Potential for pulmonary toxicity, hepatoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy, especially with long-term use; safer alternatives available." (p. 2057).

**A. Continue nitrofurantoin because long-term suppression reduces the pulmonary and hepatic toxicity risks.** Wrong, long-term use is associated with particular toxicity concern and is itself a reason for avoidance (p. 2057).
**B. Avoid nitrofurantoin because kidney function and long-term use meet avoidance criteria.** Correct, her reported clearance is below the cited threshold and the prescription is for long-term suppression, meeting both conditions (p. 2057).
**C. Continue nitrofurantoin because the avoidance criteria are independent of the level of kidney function.** Wrong, creatinine clearance is explicitly included in the avoidance criterion (p. 2057).
**D. Continue nitrofurantoin because the toxicity concerns primarily concern short courses rather than prolonged use.** Wrong, Beers emphasizes toxicity especially with long-term use, not primarily with short courses (p. 2057).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2057.

q: An 84-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and mild cognitive impairment attends routine follow-up. His daughter reports two falls during the past month, both at night while getting up to use the toilet. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, zolpidem 10 mg at bedtime, and aspirin 81 mg daily. Blood pressure is 138/82 sitting and 118/70 after three minutes standing. Which interpretation of zolpidem is consistent with Beers 2023?
o: Its association with falls supports planning discontinuation during medication review
Its nonbenzodiazepine structure supports retaining treatment despite recurrent falls
Its substantial improvement in sleep duration supports retaining treatment for insomnia
Its protection against delirium supports retaining treatment despite cognitive impairment
explanation:
**Zolpidem** is included among the hypnotics that Beers recommends avoiding. These drugs share adverse events with benzodiazepines, including falls and delirium, while producing minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration (p. 2060).
"events similar to those of benzodiazepines in older adults (e.g., delirium, falls, fractures," (p. 2060).
"minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration." (p. 2060).

**A. Its association with falls supports planning discontinuation during medication review.** Correct, it applies the avoid recommendation to a listed hypnotic in a patient with falls without identifying it as the sole cause (p. 2060; application).
**B. Its nonbenzodiazepine structure supports retaining treatment despite recurrent falls.** Wrong, nonbenzodiazepine structure does not remove the fall concern: the source describes adverse events similar to benzodiazepines (p. 2060).
**C. Its substantial improvement in sleep duration supports retaining treatment for insomnia.** Wrong, Beers describes sleep-latency and duration benefits as minimal, so the proposed justification overstates their benefit (p. 2060).
**D. Its protection against delirium supports retaining treatment despite cognitive impairment.** Wrong, delirium is a listed adverse event rather than a protective effect of zolpidem (p. 2060).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2060.

q: An 88-year-old man with mild dementia, BPH, osteoarthritis, and insomnia has become increasingly confused over three days and no longer recognizes family. One week ago he started diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime and oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily. Vital signs are stable and CAM screening is positive. Which medication plan applies Beers 2023 guidance to minimize his anticholinergic burden?
o: Discontinue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin, then reassess symptoms.
Replace diphenhydramine with oral doxylamine and continue oxybutynin.
Replace oxybutynin with oral tolterodine and continue diphenhydramine.
Continue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin while monitoring symptoms.
explanation:
**Concurrent anticholinergic drugs** increase the risk of cognitive decline, delirium, and falls or fractures. Beers lists both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as strongly anticholinergic and recommends minimizing the number of such drugs (pp. 2070, 2074). "Use of more than one medication with anticholinergic properties increases the risk of cognitive decline, delirium, and falls or fractures." (p. 2070).

**A. Discontinue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin, then reassess symptoms.** Correct, this removes both listed exposures and implements the recommendation to minimize anticholinergic drugs (pp. 2070, 2074).
**B. Replace diphenhydramine with oral doxylamine and continue oxybutynin.** Wrong, doxylamine is also strongly anticholinergic, so the substitution leaves two listed drugs in use (p. 2074).
**C. Replace oxybutynin with oral tolterodine and continue diphenhydramine.** Wrong, tolterodine is also strongly anticholinergic, so this substitution retains two listed drugs in use (p. 2074).
**D. Continue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin while monitoring symptoms.** Wrong, monitoring without reducing exposure does not implement the recommendation to minimize concurrent anticholinergic drugs (p. 2070).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2070, 2074.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2066, 2070, 2074; Tables 3, 5, 7

q: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease, depression, and chronic pain from spinal stenosis attends a medication review. His wife reports increasing daytime sedation and two near-falls. He takes carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg three times daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, gabapentin 300 mg three times daily, tramadol 50 mg four times daily, and docusate 100 mg twice daily. He also takes oral diphenhydramine 50 mg nightly for sleep. Which characteristic of diphenhydramine explains the Beers recommendation to avoid this use?
o: Accelerated clearance in advanced age, requiring higher doses to sustain a hypnotic effect.
Reduced likelihood of confusion with regular use, despite development of tolerance during treatment.
Strong anticholinergic effects and confusion risk, with cumulative exposure associated with increased falls.
Progressively enhanced hypnotic efficacy with repeated use, supporting dose reduction during continued treatment.
explanation:
The **2023 AGS Beers Criteria** recommend avoiding first-generation antihistamines, including oral diphenhydramine, for this use (Table 2, p. 2057). The rationale includes strong anticholinergic effects, reduced clearance with advanced age, and tolerance when used as a hypnotic (p. 2057). The criteria state: "Cumulative exposure to anticholinergic drugs is associated with an increased risk of falls, delirium, and dementia, even in younger adults" (p. 2057).

**A. Accelerated clearance in advanced age, requiring higher doses to sustain a hypnotic effect.** Wrong, the criteria describe reduced clearance with advanced age, not accelerated clearance that warrants a higher hypnotic dose (p. 2057).
**B. Reduced likelihood of confusion with regular use, despite development of tolerance during treatment.** Wrong, confusion is a stated anticholinergic risk; tolerance to the hypnotic effect does not supply the proposed reduction in confusion risk (p. 2057).
**C. Strong anticholinergic effects and confusion risk, with cumulative exposure associated with increased falls.** Correct, anticholinergic effects, confusion, and the association of cumulative exposure with falls explain why this nighttime use deserves review in the presented setting (p. 2057).
**D. Progressively enhanced hypnotic efficacy with repeated use, supporting dose reduction during continued treatment.** Wrong, the criteria describe tolerance developing with hypnotic use, rather than progressively enhanced hypnotic efficacy that supports ongoing treatment (p. 2057).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 2, pp. 2057.

q: A 75-year-old woman with mild dementia, hypertension, and osteoporosis has attended the emergency department three times in two months for nonspecific discomfort, with normal investigations. She takes 12 medications prescribed by four physicians, and her daughter reports increasing forgetfulness with medication-taking. Vital signs and laboratory results are normal. Which initial approach supports medication optimization?
o: Select medications to discontinue by pill count before establishing their indications
Arrange a comprehensive medication review with the patient and a pharmacist
Change dosing schedules before establishing which medications are actually taken
Add a cognitive medication before reviewing the current treatment indications
explanation:
**Comprehensive medication review** begins with an accurate account of actual use and the indication for each treatment. Hazzard emphasizes review when several prescribers are involved and simplification that preserves clinical control, rather than changes based on medication count alone (pp. 311, 313). "Medication review is required on a regular basis to determine if the medications prescribed to an older adult are appropriate for them." (p. 311)

**A. Select medications to discontinue by pill count before establishing their indications.** Wrong, the source requires reviewing actual use and indications; pill count does not identify which treatments are appropriate to stop (p. 313).
**B. Arrange a comprehensive medication review with the patient and a pharmacist.** Correct, a patient-involved comprehensive review establishes actual use, indications, and potential changes; Hazzard discusses pharmacist participation in this process (pp. 311, 313).
**C. Change dosing schedules before establishing which medications are actually taken.** Wrong, simplification is useful after understanding the regimen; changing schedules before establishing use bypasses the required review (p. 313).
**D. Add a cognitive medication before reviewing the current treatment indications.** Wrong, adding treatment before examining existing indications bypasses review and risks the therapeutic momentum described by the source (p. 313).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 311, 313.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with dementia and chronic kidney disease was hospitalized for suspected digoxin toxicity, and digoxin was withheld.
